title: Takht Hazur Sahib
hookLine: at Nanded, where he passed the Guruship to the Granth

lines: A LIFE DRAWN ACROSS A MAP.
cards: Draw a line on a map of India. Start at Patna in the east, where the Tenth Guru was born. Swing it west to Anandpur in the hills of Punjab, where the Khalsa began.

Then drop it a long way south, across the middle of the country, to a town on the Godavari river called Nanded. The line of his life ends far from where it started, and far from where most of his story happened.
You've stood at Nanded once before on this path, for his last days. Now, the place itself, and the Takht that stands there.

teach.b: Takht Hazur Sahib stands at Nanded, by the Godavari. Hazur is a word of respect for being in the presence of someone great, and Sikhs often call the place simply Hazur Sahib.
Its fuller name speaks of Sachkhand, the realm of truth, and Abchal Nagar, which Sikhs render as the steady, unmoving city. Now the history it keeps.
Tradition says that here, near the end of his life, Guru Gobind Singh named no person to follow him.

teach.h: THE GURUSHIP GIVEN TO THE GRANTH.
teach.b: He bowed before the Granth and passed the Guruship to it. From that day, Sikhs say, the Guru is the Guru Granth Sahib, with the Khalsa gathered before it as the Guru Panth.
So Patna holds the beginning of one life, and Nanded holds its end, and the beginning of something without an end. A person is born, and a person dies. The Granth was given to stay.
That's why Sikhs speak of this Takht with such weight: it marks the hand-off. It also shows how far the panth reaches.
Patna in the east and Nanded in the south both sit far from Punjab, which some readers take as a quiet reminder that the Guru's house was never meant to belong to one province.
Pilgrims come by train and bus from all over to bow where the hand-off happened.

how: Sikhs travel to Hazur Sahib in Nanded to bow where tradition says Guru Gobind Singh passed the Guruship to the Guru Granth Sahib.

games.q: you're at Nanded, near the end of the Tenth Guru's life. who will be the Guru after him?
o: the Granth, with the Khalsa gathered before it.
no one; the line simply stops.
games.why: tradition says he bowed before the Granth and passed the Guruship to it. a person can die; the Granth was given to stay.

practice: Picture a wide river moving slowly through flat land under a big southern sky, and let the water pass you without hurrying. A river can't be held in one place; it goes on after anyone who stands beside it.
If you pray, rest in the Guru's presence by the water; if you don't, let the river carry your breath along.
